questions.stem: A business stakeholder asks the team to 'build an AI agent that handles customer refunds'. What should the engineer do FIRST?
options: Pick the most capable model so the agent can handle any refund scenario.
Gather requirements first: volumes, refund limits, approval thresholds, systems of record, audit needs, success metrics.
Write a detailed system prompt describing the company's refund policy.
Build a prototype agent with full access to the refund API so that stakeholders can quickly see everything that's possible end to end.
explanations: Model choice follows from the requirements. It isn't the first step.
Correct. These requirements decide whether you need an agent at all, which tools it gets, and where humans must approve.
Useful later, but premature before you know scope, constraints and success criteria.
Giving an unscoped prototype a money-moving tool before requirements and guardrails exist is risky.

questions.stem: Anthropic announces that a model your company uses will be retired in 60 days. The model ID appears in at least 14 services owned by different teams. What should the platform team do FIRST?
options: Ask Anthropic for an extension, since 60 days isn't enough to migrate 14 services.
Run a repo-wide find-and-replace to the successor model ID and deploy it to all services this week to meet the deadline.
Nothing yet. After retirement, requests to the old ID are routed automatically to the recommended successor.
Inventory every use of the model ID, assign owners, and plan migrations with regression evals and staged rollouts.
explanations: This is the wrong first move. Start migrating now within the published timeline.
Swapping without evals or a staged rollout risks quality, format and cost regressions in all 14 services at once.
Retired models stop serving requests. Calls to them fail rather than being redirected.
Correct. You can't migrate what you haven't found. The inventory and owners make the deadline manageable and the migration testable.

questions.stem: Before switching a production extraction pipeline to a newer Claude model, the team runs a regression evaluation. Which THREE comparisons are MOST important to include? (Select THREE.)
options: Token usage per request and latency, both input/output tokens and p95 time.
Task quality on the same labeled golden set used for the current model.
Output format and schema compliance, such as the JSON parse and validation success rate.
A few manual chats in the Console to get a feel for the new model.
HTTP success rate of the new model in a staging smoke test.
Public leaderboard scores for the two models.
explanations: Correct. Tokenization and verbosity can differ between models, which changes cost and latency even at the same per-token price.
Correct. Same data, same metric is the core regression check.
Correct. A newer model can be smarter yet still break downstream parsers.
Too small and too subjective to detect regressions.
Quality regressions still return 200, so this measures availability, not quality.
Generic benchmarks don't tell you how the model does on your task and data.

questions.stem: After switching a summarization service to a newer model with the same per-token price, monthly cost rose about 25% at unchanged request volume. Quality improved, and the prompts and `max_tokens` settings are unchanged. What is the MOST likely explanation to check first?
options: The new model uses more tokens for the same work (tokenizer or verbosity); compare `usage` per request across models.
The account is still being billed at the old model's rates until the next invoice cycle.
Streaming responses cost more per token than non-streaming, and the new model streams by default.
Prompt caching stays disabled after a model change until it's re-enabled in the Console, so every request is billed uncached.
explanations: Correct. Token counts can differ between model generations for identical text, and verbosity changes output tokens. Usage data will show which one it is.
The price is the same by assumption, so a billing lag wouldn't cause an increase.
Streaming doesn't change per-token pricing, and models don't switch transport on their own.
Caches are per model, so the first requests after a switch are uncached, but caching resumes on its own. It doesn't explain a sustained 25% increase.

questions.stem: Offline evals show a new prompt plus model combination is slightly better. The service handles 2 million requests a day for paying customers. What is the BEST way to put the change into production?
options: Deploy to everyone at the lowest-traffic hour, and roll back if support tickets rise.
Canary it behind a flag to a small share of traffic, compare metrics with the control, then expand or roll back.
Ship it, since the offline eval already proved it's better.
Run the new version in a shadow environment for a full month, comparing outputs offline, before any user ever sees it.
explanations: A big-bang release exposes every user at once, and support tickets are a slow, lagging signal.
Correct. A staged rollout limits the impact and gives real-traffic evidence with a fast rollback.
Offline sets never cover all production inputs. Production validation is still needed.
Shadowing is useful, but a month with no user exposure stalls the rollout. A canary with clear gates is the better primary step.

questions.stem: Which per-request log record BEST supports debugging, cost attribution and change tracking for a Claude-backed service?
options: Request ID, model, prompt version, input/output/cache token counts, latency, `stop_reason` and error status.
The full prompt and response text only, so any issue can be reproduced.
The HTTP status code and the timestamp of each call.
A daily total of requests and spend from the billing page.
explanations: Correct. These fields support support tickets (request ID), cost attribution (usage), regression tracing (versions) and output health (`stop_reason`).
Without IDs, token counts, version or latency you can't attribute cost or trace changes, and full text raises privacy risk.
This catches outages but misses cost, truncation and which configuration produced an output.
Aggregates help with budgets but can't explain individual failures or regressions.

questions.stem: A platform team wants token and cost metrics from every engineer's Claude Code sessions sent to the company's OpenTelemetry collector, and engineers must not be able to redirect the data elsewhere. What is the BEST way to configure this?
options: Set `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY` and the `OTEL_*` exporter and endpoint variables in the managed settings `env` block that IT deploys.
Write a cron job that parses each machine's `~/.claude` session files and uploads token counts.
Commit the `OTEL_*` variables in each repository's `.claude/settings.json` so every session in the repo exports them.
Ask engineers to export the variables in their shell profiles and audit compliance quarterly.
explanations: Correct. Managed settings apply to every user, and a managed OTLP endpoint takes precedence over endpoints developers set.
Brittle and unsupported, and it duplicates the built-in OpenTelemetry export.
Claude Code ignores telemetry exporter variables in project and local settings. A repo can only turn a signal off.
Engineers can change or remove these, so nothing enforces the configuration.

questions.stem: A security reviewer asks whether turning on Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export will send developers' prompt text to the observability vendor. What is the accurate answer?
options: No. Only aggregate session counts are exported, never per-request token or cost data.
Yes. Prompt text is always included in exported events so sessions can be reconstructed.
Prompt text is exported only for sessions running in headless `-p` mode.
Not by default: prompts are redacted unless `OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1` is set.
explanations: Token and cost metrics and per-request events are exported. Only the content is redacted by default.
Prompt content isn't exported by default.
Content logging doesn't depend on interactive versus headless mode.
Correct. Content logging is opt-in, so metrics and events can flow without prompt text.

questions.stem: After a prompt update, a Q&A service's HTTP error rate and latency look normal, but users report shorter, less useful answers. The current dashboards didn't catch it. Which TWO monitoring additions would MOST directly catch this kind of regression? (Select TWO.)
options: Raise the client's `max_retries` so transient errors don't affect answers.
Extend log retention from 30 to 365 days.
Sample production requests into an automated rubric or LLM-judge evaluation, tracked by prompt version.
Add alerts on 5xx and 529 error rates with tighter thresholds.
Track the distribution of `stop_reason` (for example, the share of `max_tokens`) and output-token counts per prompt version.
explanations: Retries address transient failures, not degraded content.
Longer retention helps investigations but doesn't detect anything.
Correct. Online quality scoring catches regressions that still return HTTP 200.
Availability alerts can't see a quality regression that returns 200.
Correct. Shifts in truncation or output length are cheap, early signals of behavior change.

questions.stem: Right after a deploy, many API responses in a report generator end mid-sentence. Logs show `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` on those responses. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The API is overloaded and is cutting responses short to shed load, so the client should retry those requests with backoff.
The output budget is too small for the new responses; raise `max_tokens` or request more concise output.
A safety classifier stopped the output. Rephrase the prompt.
A stop sequence in the prompt is matching. Remove the stop sequences.
explanations: Overload returns 529 errors, not successful responses with `max_tokens`.
Correct. `max_tokens` as the stop reason means generation hit the configured cap.
That would show as a refusal stop reason, not `max_tokens`.
A stop-sequence match reports `stop_sequence`, not `max_tokens`.

questions.stem: A small number of production requests fail with intermittent 500 errors, and the team wants Anthropic support to investigate. What is the MOST useful information to include in the ticket?
options: The full application source code that builds the requests.
The organization's API key, so support can replay the failing requests.
The `request_id` values of the failing calls, with timestamps and the error responses.
A screenshot of the team's dashboard showing the error-rate spike.
explanations: Usually unnecessary and not the fastest way to locate a server-side failure.
Never share API keys. Support doesn't need them to investigate.
Correct. The request ID (in the `request-id` header and error bodies) lets support find the exact requests.
Helpful context, but support can't find specific requests from it.

questions.stem: After migrating to a newer model, regression evals show better reasoning, but the assistant now over-applies certain rules, refusing harmless edge cases and adding unrequested warnings. The prompt, written for an older model, contains many lines like 'CRITICAL: you MUST ALWAYS...'. What should the team do?
options: Roll back permanently. The newer model is less reliable for this use case.
Add more emphatic instructions, also in capitals, explicitly telling the model not to over-apply the rules in edge cases.
Re-baseline the prompt: remove the shouted legacy workarounds, state rules plainly, and re-run the evals.
Switch to a lower-capability tier, which is less sensitive to emphatic prompts.
explanations: The evals show gains elsewhere. Adjust the prompt before giving up on the migration.
Piling on emphasis tends to make overtriggering worse with models that follow instructions closely.
Correct. Newer models follow instructions more precisely, so aggressive legacy wording can cause overtriggering. Prompts need maintenance as part of migration.
This gives up quality instead of fixing the cause in the prompt.
